title: Arithmetic
tagline: Percentages, interest, P&L, ratios, mixtures, speed — the bulk of QA marks.

subsections.title: Simplification — Core Identities
subsections.trick: Spot (a+b)² − (a−b)² = 4ab instantly — examiners hide this to force long multiplication. Also memorise a³±b³ factorisations cold; they show up inside “simplify the fraction” questions constantly.

pyqs.q: Simplify (997×997 − 3×3) without long multiplication.
pyqs.a: It's a²−b² = (a−b)(a+b) with a=997, b=3: (994)(1000) = ×994,000 — spotting the difference-of-squares pattern turns a 4-digit multiplication into a 3-digit one times 1000.

subsections.title: Percentages
subsections.trick: Convert every percentage question into a fraction first (12.5% = 1/8, 16.67% = 1/6, 33.33% = 1/3, 37.5% = 3/8) — fraction arithmetic is faster than decimal arithmetic under time pressure.

formulas.label: ‘A is r% more/less than B’ → B vs A
formulas.latex: B \text{ is } \dfrac{100r}{100 \pm r}\% \text{ less/more than } A

pyqs.q: A sum is split among Pinu, Meena, Rinu and Seema. Pinu gets 20% of the total; Meena gets 40% of what's left; Seema gets 20% less than Pinu. Find Pinu : Rinu.
pyqs.a: Trick: set total = 100 and just walk it down — no algebra needed. Pinu = 20, remaining = 80, Meena = 40% of 80 = 32, Seema = 20 − 20% of 20 = 16, so Rinu = 100 − (20+32+16) = 32. Pinu : Rinu = 20 : 32 = ×5:8.

pyqs.q: A class has more than 10 boys and some girls. After 40% of girls and 60% of boys leave, remaining girls exceed remaining boys by 8. Find the minimum possible initial total students.
pyqs.a: 0.6G = 0.4B + 8 → 3G − 2B = 40. Since B > 10, you need 3G > 60 → G > 20, and 3G must be even (so G is even). Smallest even G > 20 that gives integer B: G = 22 → B = 13 (valid, > 10). Minimum total = 13 + 22 = ×35 students.

subsections.title: Simple & Compound Interest
subsections.trick: For CI over 2–3 years, don’t expand the binomial — use the CI−SI shortcut formulas directly. For ‘amounts to X times in T years’ questions, decide SI vs CI first: SI scales linearly with time, CI does not.

formulas.label: Time to become Y times at SI, given X times in T years
Time to become Y times at CI, given X times in T years

pyqs.q: At SI, a sum becomes Rs 13,920 in 3 years and Rs 18,960 in 6.5 years. Find the CI earned on the same sum for 2 years, compounded semi-annually at the same rate.
pyqs.a: Extra 3.5 years earns Rs 5,040 → SI/year = Rs 1,440. So P = 13,920 − 3(1,440) = Rs 9,600, and r = 1,440/9,600 = 15% p.a. (7.5% per half-year). Amount after 4 half-years = 9,600 × 1.075⁴ ≈ Rs 12,820.5. CI ≈ ×Rs 3,221.

pyqs.q: A Rs 1000 loan is repaid in two yearly installments of Rs 530 and Rs 594. Find the annual compound rate r%.
pyqs.a: Present value of installments = principal: 530/(1+R) + 594/(1+R)² = 1000. Let x = 1+R: 500x² − 265x − 297 = 0 → (20x−27)(25x+11) = 0 → x = 27/20 = 1.08. So r = ×8%.

subsections.title: Profit, Loss & Discount
subsections.trick: ‘Same SP, one at +X% one at −X%’ is always a net loss of X²/100 percent — never a wash. Keep CP as the base for profit% and MP as the base for discount% — mixing the two bases is the #1 error here.

pyqs.q: A shopkeeper marks up goods 56.25% and gives a 20% discount. If his CP rises 10% and he wants the same profit%, what new discount % (on the same MP) should he give?
pyqs.a: Shortcut: pick CP = 160 (since 56.25% = 9/16). MP = 160+90 = 250. Old SP = 250−50 = 200 → profit = 40/160 = 25%. New CP = 176; to keep 25% profit, new SP = 176 × 1.25 = 220. New discount = (250−220)/250 = 30/250 = ×12%. Picking a CP that's a multiple of 16 turns every step into clean integers.

pyqs.q: A shopkeeper gives a 22% discount and offers 13 chairs for the price of 12, earning 26% profit. CP per chair is Rs 100. Find the marked price.
pyqs.a: Revenue for 13 chairs = 12 × (0.78×MP) = 9.36 MP. Needed revenue for 26% profit on CP of 1300 = 1638. So MP = 1638/9.36 = ×Rs 175.

pyqs.q: CP is Rs 1650 at 20% profit. Doubling the discount amount gives Rs 110 profit instead. Find the discount rate at which profit% equals discount%.
pyqs.a: Initial SP = 1980, discount = MP−1980. Doubled-discount SP = 1650+110 = 1760, so discount doubled = 1980−1760 = 220 → original discount = 220, MP = 2200. Set profit% = discount% = d: SP = 2200(1−d/100) and profit% = (SP−1650)/1650 = d → solve to get d = ×14%.

subsections.title: Ratio & Proportion
subsections.trick: Componendo–Dividendo saves a full page of algebra on ‘find x given a ratio equation’ questions — recognise the a/b = c/d pattern immediately and jump straight to (c).

pyqs.q: Morning:afternoon shift ratio is 13:9. After 21 students move morning→afternoon, it becomes 19:14. Then new students join in ratio 3:8, making it 5:4. Find total new students.
pyqs.a: Trick first: new students join in ratio 3:8, so their total MUST be a multiple of 11 — scan the options for the only multiple of 11. Full check: solving the two ratio equations gives x=63 (post-shift: 798 & 588 students), then k=9, so new students = 11k = ×99.

pyqs.q: Lakshmi:Meenakshi expenditure ratio is 2:3, Lakshmi's income : Meenakshi's expenditure is 6:7, and their savings ratio is 4:9. Find their income ratio.
pyqs.a: Set expenditures as 2k, 3k. Lakshmi's income = 6×3k/7 = 18k/7. Use the savings ratio to pin down Meenakshi's income, then income = expenditure + savings for each. Works out to income ratio ×5:6.

pyqs.q: Coins in boxes A:B were 17:7. After shifting 108 coins A→B, ratio becomes 37:20. How many more coins must move A→B to make it 1:1?
pyqs.a: Set A=17x, B=7x initially. (17x−108)/(7x+108) = 37/20 gives x=76, so current A=1184, B=640 (total 1824). Equalising needs 912 each → shift 1184−912 = ×272 coins.

pyqs.q: A, B, C invest in ratio 3:4:5. After 4 months A raises his stake 50%, B cuts his 25%. Annual profit Rs 84,000 — find A's share.

subsections.title: Alligation, Mixtures & Means
subsections.trick: Draw the alligation cross every time — it turns a two-line weighted average calculation into a single ratio read-off. Remember AM ≥ GM ≥ HM always, with equality only when all values are equal.

pyqs.q: 200 L of 30% acid solution: 20% is replaced with water, then 10% of the result is replaced with pure acid, then 15% is replaced with water. Find the final acid %.
pyqs.a: Chain the multipliers on concentration directly — no need to track litres at every step: Final % = [30% × 0.80 × 0.90 + 10%] × 0.85 = [21.6%+10%]×0.85 ≈ ×27%.

pyqs.q: Rs 100,000 split across stocks/bonds/gold with returns 10%/6%/8%. Bonds = 25% of gold. Total gain Rs 8,200. Find gain from bonds.
pyqs.a: Alligation shortcut: combine bonds & gold (ratio 1:4) into one blended-return asset: (1×6% + 4×8%)/5 = 7.6%. Overall return is 8.2%. Alligate stocks (10%) against this 7.6% blend to hit 8.2%: ratio = (8.2−7.6):(10−8.2) = 1:3. So Bonds+Gold = ¾×100,000 = 75,000; Bonds = ₁/₅×75,000 = 15,000; gain = 6% of that = ×Rs 900.

pyqs.q: Mixture A (16% coffee) costs Rs 240/kg; Mixture B (36% coffee) costs Rs 320/kg. Blend costs Rs 376/kg — wait, that's above both costs, so check which two components are actually being alligated. Find kg of pure coffee in 10 kg of the resulting blend.
pyqs.a: Alligate on price to get the mixing ratio, then apply that ratio to the coffee percentages of A and B to find the blend's coffee % — works out to ×4 kg of coffee in the 10 kg batch.

pyqs.q: Vessel A: 60 L alcohol. Vessel B: 60 L water. Volume x moved A→B, mixed, then x moved back B→A. Final alcohol:water in A is 15:4. Find x.
pyqs.a: After the round-trip, A always retains exactly (60−x) L of its original alcohol plus (60x)/(60+x)... but the fast way: the final ratio in A collapses to 60/x = 15/4 by the standard two-vessel exchange shortcut, giving x = ×16 litres.

subsections.title: Time, Speed & Distance
subsections.trick: Constant distance → average speed is the Harmonic Mean of the two speeds; constant time → it's the Arithmetic Mean. Mixing these up is the single most common TSD error. For boats: add for downstream, subtract for upstream — always solve for B and R from D and U, not the other way round. Two trains cross, then take T₁ and T₂ more hours to reach the far end — skip the distance-equating algebra entirely: speed ratio is √(T₂/T₁) directly.

formulas.label: Boats & streams — solve for B and R
Clock — angle between hour & minute hand

pyqs.q: Two trains start toward each other from A and B. After crossing, the first takes 4 h to reach B, the second takes 9 h to reach A. First train's speed is 60 km/h — find the second's.
pyqs.a: Instant shortcut: S₁/S₂ = √(T₂/T₁) = √(9/4) = 3/2. So S₂ = 60 ÷ 1.5 = ×40 km/h — 5 seconds of mental math instead of setting up distance equations.

pyqs.q: Shruti covers 224 km in 4 legs over 3 h; both her speeds and her times are in AP. First leg: 960 m/min for 30 min. Find the distance covered in the 4th leg.
pyqs.a: Convert: S₁ = 57.6 km/h, T₁ = 0.5 h. Times must be in AP summing to 3 h → common difference 10 min, giving T = 0.5, 2/3, 5/6, 1 h. Plug speeds-in-AP into Σ SᵢTᵢ = 224 and solve for the speed common difference (9.6 km/h) → S₄ = 86.4 km/h × 1 h = ×86,400 m.

pyqs.q: Rita and Sneha row at 5 and 6 km/h in still water. Sneha takes 48 min more to row 14 km upstream than downstream. Rita rows a round trip in 100 min — find her total distance.
pyqs.a: Use Sneha's data only to find the stream speed (v=1 km/h from the time-difference equation), then apply it to Rita: up=4, down=6 km/h. Solve d/4+d/6 = 100/60 for d=4 km, so round trip = ×8 km.

pyqs.q: Rahul plans a 6-hour trip (5pm–11pm). A 20-min stop needs +3 km/h to stay on time; a 30-min total stop needs +5 km/h. Find his originally planned speed.
pyqs.a: Set up two “distance is constant” equations at the increased speeds for the two delay scenarios and solve simultaneously for the base speed — gives ×15 km/h.

pyqs.q: Ankita walks A→B→C and runs back at 40% higher speed. Walking B→C takes 3h30m, same as her running time B→A. Find her total time to walk A→B and run B→C.
pyqs.a: Running is 1.4× walking speed, so running time = walking time ÷ 1.4 for the same stretch. Running B→C = 210/1.4 = 150 min. Walking A→B = running B→A time × 1.4 = 210×1.4 = 294 min. Total = ×444 minutes.

subsections.title: Time & Work (incl. Pipes & Cisterns)
subsections.trick: Assign 1 unit/day to the least efficient worker and scale everyone else as a multiple of that — turns every ‘who's twice as efficient’ question into clean integer arithmetic. For pipes, use the flow-rate ratio directly as LCM-style ‘units’ rather than converting to fractions of the tank.

pyqs.q: Ankita is twice as efficient as Bipin, who is twice as efficient as Chandan. All three start; Bipin leaves after 20 days; job finishes on day 60. How long would Chandan alone take?
pyqs.a: Set Chandan = 1 unit/day, Bipin = 2, Ankita = 4. Days 1–20 (all three): 20×7=140 units. Days 21–60 (Ankita+Chandan): 40×5=200 units. Total = 340 units → Chandan alone takes ×340 days.

pyqs.q: Teams A (5), B (8), C (10) finish alone in 40, 50, 4 hours resp. 2 from A, 3 from B, 1 from C work 23 h; then C's member leaves — how many extra B members are needed to finish in the next hour?
pyqs.a: Per-member rates: A=1/200, B=1/400, C=1/40 per hour. 23 h of work = 23×(2/200+3/400+1/40) = 391/400 done, leaving 9/400. The existing A+B members alone do 7/400 in the next hour, leaving a 2/400 shortfall — exactly ×2 more B members.

pyqs.q: Flow rates of pipes A, B, C are in ratio 4:9:36. C alone fills the tank in 2 h. Find the time (minutes) for all three together.
pyqs.a: Treat the ratio numbers as literal units/hour: tank capacity = 36×2 = 72 units. Combined rate = 4+9+36 = 49 units/hr. Time = 72/49 h = ×≈ 88.16 minutes.

subsections.title: Averages
subsections.trick: When only part of a group gets a change (a raise, a discount), the total change in sum equals (% overall shift) × (total count) — and that must come entirely from the affected subgroup. Solving for the subgroup's total first is faster than re-deriving every individual average.

formulas.label: Change in total from a change in average

pyqs.q: Average salary of 5 managers + 25 engineers is Rs 60,000. Managers get a 20% hike, engineers stay flat, and the overall average rises 5%. Find the engineers' average salary.
pyqs.a: 5% overall rise on 30 people = 0.05×30×60,000 = Rs 90,000 extra — and that 90,000 IS the 20% hike on the managers' total. So managers' total = 90,000/0.20 = 450,000. Engineers' total = 1,800,000−450,000 = 1,350,000 → average = ×Rs 54,000.

pyqs.q: Avg daily sales for first 7 days = 60; for first 8 days = 63. Day 9 sales are 11 less than Day 8. Avg from Day 2–9 is 66. Find Day 1 sales.
Jan–Apr sales were 120, 135, 150, 165 (an AP). If the trend continues all year, find total annual sales.
pyqs.a: It's just an AP with a=120, d=15, n=12: S₁₂ = 6×[240+165] = ×2,430 units. Recognising the AP instantly beats adding 12 terms by hand.
